title: How yield is defined
summary: Yield is harvested production divided by harvested area, reported in kg per hectare, and is crop-specific.
text: Yield is the harvested production of a crop divided by the harvested area of that crop. It is reported in kilograms per hectare (kg/ha), or tonnes per hectare (t/ha) where the national series uses that unit. Yield is crop-specific: maize, beans, cassava, banana and potato have very different natural yield scales, so a yield is never averaged across crops and a cross-crop 'average yield' is not produced. Yield is an observation about a season and a place, not a target and not a prediction.

title: How production and area are defined
summary: Production is reported in metric tonnes; harvested area is the area actually harvested, distinct from cultivated area.
text: Production is the quantity harvested, reported in metric tonnes. Harvested area is the area that was actually harvested, reported in hectares. Cultivated area is the area planted or cultivated, which can exceed harvested area when a crop is lost or not fully harvested. The two area measures are not interchangeable and are labelled explicitly wherever they appear. National totals are published national series; a national figure is never computed by summing district rows.

title: How the productivity gap is computed
summary: Gap index = 100 x (national crop median yield - observed district yield) / national crop median yield.
text: The productivity gap compares a district's observed yield for a crop against a benchmark: the national median yield for the same crop in the same period. The gap index is computed as 100 times (benchmark yield minus observed yield) divided by benchmark yield. A positive gap index means the district's observed yield is below the national crop median; a negative value means it is above. The benchmark strategy materially changes the reported gap, so the strategy is always stated. The gap is an association with local conditions and practices; it is not proof that changing any single factor would close it.

title: How district rankings are produced
summary: Districts are ranked by gap index, descending, for one crop and period.
text: A crop's district ranking orders districts by their gap index, from the largest gap to the smallest, for one crop in one period. A larger gap index means the observed yield sits further below the national crop median. A ranking is a prioritisation for investigation, not a causal claim and not an investment recommendation; districts with more observations and larger areas may also be more reliably measured.

title: Indexed comparisons
summary: When crops with different yield scales are compared over time, each series is indexed to a common base rather than compared in raw units.
text: Because crops have different natural yield scales, comparing raw yields across crops can be misleading. For change over time, each crop's series is indexed to a common base period so that the shape of change is comparable. Indexed values show relative movement, not absolute tonnage, and the base period is always stated. Indexed comparisons are never presented as raw yields.

title: How practice associations are measured
summary: Associations are correlations between district practice adoption and observed yield; they are never causal effects.
text: Practice associations measure how a district's reported adoption of an input or practice tracks with its observed yield, using a correlation across published district observations. Adoption is reported as a share of farmers, not of area. A positive association means districts that adopt more of the practice also tend to show a higher yield; it does not mean the practice causes the difference. These figures describe associations and are used to suggest what to investigate, never to claim an effect.

title: How post-harvest shares are interpreted
summary: Post-harvest figures are national crop-level percentages of production for sold, consumed, stored and lost amounts.
text: The post-harvest use table records how national crop output was used after harvest: sold, kept for household consumption, stored, kept as seed, used as fodder, reported as post-harvest loss, and other use, each as a percentage of production. These are national crop-level values and carry no district dimension. Shares describe composition; they are not additive with one another unless they account for the full output, and a percentage is never shown as a count.

title: How model outputs are labelled
summary: Model outputs are always labelled as modelled, carry their validation metrics, and are never presented as observations.
text: Cropmatics separates observed facts, derived indicators and modelled outputs. A modelled value is the output of a fitted model and is always labelled as modelled wherever it appears, together with the model card's validation metrics and training context. Model outputs should not be read as predictions of a specific future value, and they are never substituted for a published observation. Where a model is not registered, no modelled figure is shown.

title: Policy on missing data
summary: A missing value is reported as missing, never as zero; a period with no rows is absent, not empty.
text: When a value is not published for a selection, it is reported as missing and never coerced to zero, because a zero would be read as a real measured zero. A period that has no rows is presented as not published rather than as an empty success, and a dataset that covers only one release explains that honestly when another period is selected. Requesting a period that was never published is an error, not an empty result.

title: Source and provenance policy
summary: Every figure carries a source id and period; PostgreSQL is the production authority and the model is never a source of facts.
text: Every figure Cropmatics shows carries the source it came from and the period it describes. The analytical authority is the canonical database, with the processed pipeline files as a reproducibility and fallback layer; which layer answered a read is reported. A language model never produces a numerical observation: figures come only from controlled tools, and any figure an answer states must be traceable to retrieved evidence or the answer is rejected and the verified explanation is returned instead.

title: What Cropmatics cannot answer
summary: Market prices, weather and rainfall are not in the dataset, so those questions are refused rather than approximated.
text: Cropmatics answers from published agricultural statistics. Market prices, input costs, credit, weather and rainfall are not part of that dataset, so questions about them are refused rather than answered with a neighbouring production figure. Refusing honestly is preferred to substituting a related statistic, because a plausible but wrong number is worse than a clear 'not available'.

title: Season definitions and comparisons
summary: A period is year plus season (YYYYA/B/C); the honest comparison is the same season one year earlier.
text: A published period is a year and a season, written as a four-digit year followed by A, B or C (for example 2026B). Seasons differ agronomically, so stepping from Season A to Season B is not a time series and must not be read as one. The comparable statement is the same season one year earlier (for example 2026B against 2025B). That comparison is made only when both observations are published; a missing baseline is reported as unavailable, never as a zero percent change.

title: Data coverage and single-release datasets
summary: District crop productivity carries every published period; input, irrigation and erosion tables are a single 2025 Season B release.
text: The district crop productivity panel carries district rows for every published period. The district input and practice, irrigation and erosion tables are a single release covering 2025 Season B only, so selecting another period returns no rows for them and the answer says so rather than borrowing the 2025B values. National crop trends and post-harvest use tables provide national context and are labelled as national.

title: Glossary of core terms
summary: Yield = umusaruro; production = umusaruro wose; area = ubutaka; improved seed = imbuto nziza; fertilizer = ifumbire.
text: Yield (umusaruro) is production per unit harvested area. Production (umusaruro) is the harvested quantity in metric tonnes. Harvested area (ubutaka bwasaruwe) is the harvested extent in hectares. Improved seed (imbuto nziza), inorganic fertilizer (ifumbire y'ubukorikori), organic fertilizer (ifumbire kama) and irrigation (kuhira) are reported as shares of farmers who reported using them. A productivity gap (itandukaniro ry'umusaruro) is the shortfall of a district's observed yield against the national crop median.

title: Frequently asked questions
summary: Cropmatics answers questions about published Rwandan agricultural statistics for the periods it covers, with sources and limitations.
text: Cropmatics answers questions about published Rwandan agricultural statistics: crop productivity, input and practice adoption, irrigation, erosion control and post-harvest use, for the periods it covers. It can compare crops, districts and periods, rank districts by gap, explain a trend and show where a number came from. It cannot answer questions about prices, weather or individual farms, and it always states the source, period and limitations of an answer. Numbers are never invented and are always shown with the evidence behind them.
